TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
THURSDAY, 13 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 8, DAY 7
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH ZELIE HEGER SC, TAMARA
PHILLIPS, MATT SHERMAN AND ALISON HAMMOND, COUNSEL
ASSISTING

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Sherman.
MR SHERMAN: Commissioner, I call Mr Lee Brennan.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Mr Brennan, will you take an oath or make an affirmation?
MR BRENNAN: Affirmation, please.
<LEE BRENNAN, AFFIRMED
COMMISSIONER: Yes, do sit down. Thank you.
MR SHERMAN: Mr Brennan, you have provided a statement dated 27 July 2026; is that
correct?
MR BRENNAN: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: Commissioner, that statement bears the document ID
STAT.8999.0001.0609, if I could tender that statement.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the statement will be admitted as an exhibit.
MR SHERMAN: Mr Brennan, you are the Chief Executive Officer of ReRoute Australia; is
that correct?
MR BRENNAN: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: You have held that role since 2024; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: You hold post-graduate qualifications in psychology, counter-terrorism
and criminology?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: In terms of your work experience, could you tell us about your role in
forensic intervention and forensic mental health in the last 15 years?
MR BRENNAN: Definitely. So I commenced working initially as a worker, a Community
Corrections officer, in the Department of Justice before moving on to work as a high-risk
assessor for the court services, so doing pre and post-release forensic mental health
assessments, before moving to do work with the high-risk sex offender program. I worked
within - a practitioner and a team leader within the family violence sector before most

recently moving over to work within the countering violent extremism and counter-terrorism
work within Victoria.
MR SHERMAN: And focusing on that most recent experience in countering violent
extremism, could you tell us what that work involved?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, definitely. So my work initially was with Victoria Police developing
and implementing Victoria's response to what was at the time referred to as right-wing
extremism and currently referred to as ideologically-motivated violent extremism. So my role
involved doing the research implementation and continued monitoring of that program with
the Counter-Terrorism Command at Victoria Police before also going on to work within the
Major Offenders Unit at Department of Justice and Community Safety, managing the
countering violent extremism prisoners within the Correctional Services.
MR SHERMAN: Now, just returning for a moment to that name change from right-wing
extremism to ideologically motivated extremism, why did that name change occur?
MR BRENNAN: My understanding during the time, there was a recommendation from the
federal government, especially from ASIO, in regards to incorporating all different forms of
extremism because when we were looking at what was initially at the time referred to as
right-wing extremism, that looked away from potentially some of the other motivations for
extremism, be it left-wing motivation, separatist networks and then also for a bit more of
those nihilistic ones, that may have not have actually incorporated under that right wing, they
might not have held a right-wing viewpoint or a right-wing motivation for undertaking
extremist actions, so they incorporate under the terminology of ideologically motivated
violent extremism.
MR SHERMAN: In terms of your work in CVE in the Major Offenders Unit, could you
explain what that particular work involved?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, definitely. So my work there was one of the system managers, so I
worked under the senior manager there to do the assessments and monitoring of CVE
prisoners within the State of Victoria. So when we had individuals that might have been
either on continued detention orders or currently serving a period of incarceration, our role
was to do the continued assessments and reporting of their progress and also monitoring their
risks within that correctional environment and make recommendations up to the relevant
bodies around that sort of continued risk and any areas that we might need to focus on.
MR SHERMAN: So is it fair to say, then, that in the course of your career prior to joining
ReRoute, you'd really worked in a broad spectrum of touch points for people involved in
extremist behaviours; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: In your statement, you distinguish between religiously-motivated
extremist conduct and ideologically-motivated extremist conduct or views. Could you explain
those two concepts?

MR BRENNAN: Yes, definitely. So when we are referring to religiously-motivated violent
extremism, it's referring to a motivation that might be based off a pre-existing religion or a
pre-existing religious movement, so potentially ones that we may have seen for some of our
groups that that we might refer to as ISIS groups or those sort of other groups there that
have - using religious connotations or religious text as that sort of overarching motivation
piece, and it will often be that reference point for them, that they might use that text or any of
those sort of religious texts there as that basis point for it. And they want to continue on with
that religious method or methodology as that sort of overarching thing.
But when we are referring to ideologically-motivated, this might be from a more - either
a social movement or a movement that's based on predominantly in the past what they have
referenced is the Neo-Nazi movements and using those more social-driven aspects for it and
that ideology of attacking for a specific group, attacking for a specific belief system or
a - even a gender ideology. And they'll actually use that rather than looking at that basis for
a religious text that might have existed previously.
MR SHERMAN: And, in your observation, are there types of extremism that don't fall into
those two categories?
MR BRENNAN: I believe that we've got a lot better in regards to actually putting them
under one. So, in the past, we have had ones - we might look at some of those more separatist
networks, we might look at those more nihilistic sort of movements there, or even the incel
movements in the past, we didn't actually look at characterising. But I believe there are ones
that we are moving a lot more towards that. I know that there's been quite extensive work to
try and align them.
I believe it's more around a fluid movement, I would probably sort of elaborate, for that one,
is in regards to - we often have a range of difficulties where people might take aspects of
different either religiously motivated or ideologically motivated and actually shift in and out
between them, and that is sort of the area that I think there needs to be a bit more focus on.
MR SHERMAN: And I understand from your statement that you have also done some work
internationally; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, that's correct.
MR SHERMAN: Including as an expert panel member for EXIT Deutschland? Could you
tell us what that work involved?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, definitely. So my work there was to do consulting and also an expert
panel member for international panels where we drew together experiences from a range of
international programs to go to discuss what they saw as the key drivers or the key current
concerns in regards to countering violent extremism. So we drew together a range of different
providers from Europe, the USA, and then also from Asian continents as well as Australia, to
look at having together a response to some of the issues we had. So one of the ones that we
sort of looked at for that one was the use of formers within work within CVE. So when we

refer to "formers", it's someone that has either exited out of a previous ideological movement
or religious movement, is now trying to reintegrate back into the community, so utilising their
knowledge and experience to actually help and assist to develop programs.
Another one that we looked at was also around the impacts of digital footprints in regards to
individuals disengaging from extremist pathways. So this one looked at whether or not these
were actually seen as a barrier, whether or not they could actually impede on someone in
being able to disengage from a program, effectively. And then we also looked at in regards to
a range of different other aspects for it in regards to the community involvement and the
responsibility of communities and community networks in regards to assisting individuals
from disengaging from extremist pathways.
MR SHERMAN: Thank you. And in your statement, you speak about your role as chief
executive of ReRoute. Could you tell us how ReRoute came to be formed and what it does as
an organisation?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, definitely. So ReRoute is a program at the moment that was
developed by our now chief operations officer. So Andrew Reynolds had identified a gap
between the existing areas within the CVE space - so what we were sort of looking at is
around that a lot of the programs that exist at the moment are focused on the higher-end
threshold when it comes to individuals becoming involved within, or becoming recognised as
being involved within a ideologically-motivated or religiously-motivated extremist network,
whereas a lot of the work that is actually required to be done is around that early intervention
phase and providing that early intervention for individuals. So Andrew did extensive work
initially in 2023 to develop ReRoute and actually start to implement some of these things in
the background.
So I initially came on as a consultative approach, due to my experience and my background
within working within the forensic interventions area and as well as CVE, to provide Andrew
with some background and some sort of frameworks to start to develop the programs
from - and from there, it really shifted into an area of focusing on providing that early
intervention space and that early intervention for individuals that might be in that sort of
initial stages of engaging within CVE or engaging within a recognised
ideologically-motivated group. So we started to look at ways that we could provide this and
actually implement areas that we could assist what were the current network.
So we didn't want to sort of look at a way that we could move away from the existing
networks that we had there, so especially with the policing-led programs, and actually look
away so we could support that. So ways that we could provide that off-ramp for a lot of
individuals before they got to need to actually have that. But also as well provide a safe and
stable and probably a less threatening approach for individuals to actually engage in or start
develop these programs. Because what we sort of found initially during our time is where
parents, family members or even peer networks were required to make referrals through to
either policing service or even through to what they saw as a national counter-terrorism
program, it was quite daunting for them to engage in that.

It was often something they didn't want to do because they didn't feel as though they had
already met that threshold where they would be able to sort of receive a policing or what they
might see as a punitive approach. So this actually provided a sort of initial one that they could
refer to and actually become involved. And then as well, that has also developed further into
our programs for looking at upskilling and providing that sort of education and training for
those working within the field, especially in those cross-sectors such as other forensic
programs, be it family violence, be it substance use programs or even youth justice programs,
where they could actually receive some consultation and support and some training about the
work that we're doing and how it might be able to empower onto their programs.
MR SHERMAN: And I think in your statement you distinguish or you identify a service gap
that you have sought to fill between what you refer to as low-level responses and the high
threshold policing and counter-terror responses that you have just been discussing. When
you're referring to lower-level responses, what are you referring to in that context?
MR BRENNAN: So when we are referring to that, what we are referring to is what they
might be in regards to that low-level antisocial behaviour. So it might be, especially when we
are looking at within a schooling-related environment, it might be the use of existing
materials. It might be in regards to the use of recognised symbols to cause a bit of concern or
a bit of discourse within that sort of schooling environment. It might be that sort of initial test
phase for them where they're sort of looking to make that impact or making that shock value,
or as well as starting to initially engage with programs outside of schools or groups outside of
schooling environments where they are - put themselves at risk of engaging in it, but they're
not actively sorting out - or not actively sort of disparaging and saying that they're going to
engage in violence or any sort of criminal behaviour for -
COMMISSIONER: Mr Brennan, can you give some concrete examples of what you're
talking about when you spoke of low-level antisocial behaviour and the content of things that
young people were reading? If you can just explain to us in a concrete way what you mean?
MR BRENNAN: Yes. So when I'm referring to that, what I'm referring to is - examples in
the past that I have witnessed or that sort of our practitioners have witnessed, is the utilisation
and bringing of recognised ideologically-motivated symbols such as swastikas or wearing or
even engaging with material such as bringing the novel - sorry, not novel, the text of Mein
Kampf to those sort of environments. Referencing those sorts of texts and referencing those
sort of experiences in the past to create a bit of a discourse within that sort of school
environment, and also actively engaging in what they might see as graffitiing sort of, and we
have sort of looked at that, so where they've looked to actually bring some of those things
into a public domain to actually cause a bit of distress or a bit of discourse out there in those
environments.
MR SHERMAN: And so ReRoute saw an opportunity to position itself between the kind of
low-level responses you might see, for example, in a school context and the more extreme
police interventions at the other end of the spectrum; is that a fair characterisation?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.

MR SHERMAN: In terms of your relationship with law enforcement and the justice system,
do you maintain relationships with police? Is that something that the organisation does?
MR BRENNAN: We maintain ones that we are sort of able to develop. So we have done
extensive work especially engaging with sort of the youth officers and some of those priority
communities areas within Victoria. So we try and maintain those networks. We've found it
difficult to be able to engage with probably more the target areas that we would like to
become engaged with, so when we are referring to the more high-level commands within
Victoria Police, we find it hard to do that. But we try and maintain extensive networks and
extensive relationships with those that we have had those direct areas, on as well as
maintaining areas where we can have reporting pathways where we do notice escalation. So
we have worked to develop reporting points and escalation points if we were to notice an
escalation in someone's behaviour, to make sure that we can sort of push that through and
receive a response in that way.
MR SHERMAN: You have obviously had a very extensive experience in law enforcement.
Are there any practical barriers that you have observed in terms of getting access to
high-level commands or developing those relationships where - particular things that have
caused problems?
MR BRENNAN: I believe what has been a particular barrier in that sort of situation and
what has always been in the past is in regards to the information-sharing pathways and also
being able to actually gain what you might receive as a foothold in regards to engage in those
ones. Because what we are looking at, especially from a community-led approach, there's
sometimes a pre-existing notion around the work that can be done and the work that can sort
of be undertaken from a community-led aspect, versus an actual police intervention program.
And when we are looking at gaining into those relationships and gaining that sort of level of
what I refer to as that respect or recognition of those programs, especially in very early days,
it can be quite a challenge to actually develop those partnerships.
And one thing I recognised in the past and why I sort of came on in the role is if you don't
actually have potentially inside knowledge or inside experience within that, from someone
from the outside, especially when Andrew started initially within the role and initially tried to
get ReRoute to be implemented, it was very difficult to find areas that he could communicate
with or potential networks that he could actually engage with at that time.
MR SHERMAN: You have obviously given some evidence a little earlier about the
importance of community-led organisations in terms of a point of access that the not
securitised or associated with the police. Are there any other benefits, to your mind, of the
involvement of communication organisations in this space?
MR BRENNAN: Definitely. I feel as though that once we are sort of able to implement these
community-led approaches and we are actually able to implement these lower-level responses
for it, the first one as well is actually able to engage with those that we might have seen in the
past that have actually an anti-establishment or an anti-government led approach. Because in
the past, a lot of times we've seen individuals have outright refused or sort of disengaged
from existing programs because they've held a belief system or they've held an ideology

around that governments are around to actually just keep them down. They're just there to
sort of continue to suppress their viewpoint. So what we're sort of looking at programs that
are led by either government led, justice led or policing interventions, it can sometimes
reiterate some of those ideologies they might have or further entrench them into the belief
system that the programs being offered aren't actually in a way that can be for this individual
to be able to engage or this individual to actually seek that sort of support.
Whereas when we are looking at a community-led approach and the sort of community one,
we are actually able to foster some of those relationships within the communities. We are
actually able sort of break down some of these barriers for people engaging into it. As well as
we are able to also utilise a lot of the knowledge and experience in the community. Because
a disengagement program, especially a disengagement process for a lot of individuals, it
involves a wraparound service, as we like to say. It involves those that are close to them
becoming heavily involved into that process and invested into that process. And ultimately
when we have individuals or communities involved in these processes, they're able to provide
that help, that sort of support, as well as we're able to utilise some of the existing knowledge
and experience that we can look at to sort of incorporate into that disengagement program for
them as well.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. And in terms of the government-based programs, you would
obviously accept that there's a role for those programs, wouldn't you?
MR BRENNAN: Definitely.
MR SHERMAN: In the case of particularly violent offenders or particularly risky offenders,
there's obviously a role for police and those type of disengagement programs in this area?
MR BRENNAN: Definitely. I believe that they are crucial in regards to and especially when
it becomes - there is a need to recognise that especially community-led programs do have
a threshold in regards to how they are able to engage when we are referring to especially
areas of national security or an action or where we're sort of escalating to a point an
individual might be looking at taking on a violent action. That is very much an area that I
think needs to be held at that higher level and at that sort of policing-led intervention whereas
our ones are looking at areas that we can involve at that lower level.
COMMISSIONER: How are clients referred to ReRoute?
MR BRENNAN: So we have several ways that a client can be referred to it. We have often
had in the past during a secondary consultation with another provider, so we provide quite
extensive secondary consultation and training programs -
COMMISSIONER: What does secondary consultation mean?
MR BRENNAN: So secondary consultation refers to when we might have, say, another
community organisation that might be dealing with a person that they have some concerns
about but they don't actually have that existing knowledge and experience about working
with these individuals. They might seek our services out to actually provide a brief education

piece, as well as reviewing that case where we can help to identify what we might see as
existing risk factors or existing areas that we could provide intervention service from. So a
secondary consultation refers to our ability to review a case and provide that sort of guidance
for another area that might not have that existing knowledge and experience.
COMMISSIONER: Apart from referrals from other organisations, is there any other means
that ReRoute gets its clients?
MR BRENNAN: Yes. So we have a direct referral service. So we have - part of our website,
we have the ability for parents, peers or anyone to sort of make a direct referral from,
whereas the majority of referrals do come from that direct referral source, as well as any sort
of ones that we might have if we have existing relationships to other service providers that
may have engaged with us - be it the training, secondary consultation or even another
intervention that we might have been delivering, they can also make referrals through to our
organisation.
COMMISSIONER: How are you funded?
MR BRENNAN: We are currently in a lot of areas self-funded, so executive-level
contributions, as well as for areas that we might have had for external donations for it. We
have sought out to have ongoing funding, however that has been a particular difficulty in the
past.
MR SHERMAN: Do you have a copy of your statement there in front of you?
MR BRENNAN: Yes, I do.
MR SHERMAN: I might take you to paragraph 17 to ask you some questions about the
organisation, if that's okay. Do you have that paragraph up?
MR BRENNAN: I do.
MR SHERMAN: So you will see there that the ReRoute is structured into two different
divisions; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: Could you just explain briefly what the Director of Forensic Interventions
Channel is responsible for?
MR BRENNAN: Definitely. So the Director of Forensic Interventions really focuses on our
intervention programs as well as our proactive program. So you will see in regards to later
within the statement, there is the definition of those programs. So they're really looking at
that direct support and that sort of direct work that we might be doing. So when some
individual is referred into the program, that side of the program is really focused on provision
of that direct support, that direct intervention programs, as well as the continued risk
assessments and sort of those continued risk reporting frameworks that they work towards.

So you will see on there we have the Manager of the Risk and Needs Assessment, as well at
our forensic practitioners. So these are the ones that do our analysis and do the continued risk
assessments, as well as they do six-monthly as well as 12-monthly reviews of a participant
within the program. So they might do check-ins, as well as sort of measure how the
individual might be going within the programs. And then for our major interventions, they are
really focused on doing that sort of direct on the ground analysis and direct on the ground
monitoring of those people in the program. So we have our case managers and mentors who
will be providing that direct support to individuals that are referred to the program.
And our Director of Strategy and Insights Pathways, that is looking for the secondary
consultation programs, those sort of direct training ones, as well as our school-based
programs. As well there, you will see for our community engagement partnerships, this is
really focused on developing those sort of stakeholder relationships, developing those sort of
networks out there in the community and developing some of those partner programs that we
might have that can ultimately assist in regards to doing a lot of programs that we do. So
what it does and we sort of look at that and why was it divided up in those two ones, is we
have a real strategy and oversight as well as that education training aspect, and the other side
of it is really looking at that direct intervention and that on the groundwork being done.
MR SHERMAN: And is the split on the aqua side between the risk and needs assessments
and the interventions a deliberate risk management strategy?
MR BRENNAN: Correct. We wanted to have an element of sort of - I'd say disconnection
between those two so that it could be really impartial when we are doing those sort of work.
So they do communicate. They do share communication. But there is a level of impartiality
between the two of them so that the assessments aren't going to be based on any sort of
engagements they might be having or any sort of relationships that the case managers might
be having with the worker - I mean, with the individuals that are referred, and then it has that
level where they do have that disconnection from it.
MR SHERMAN: And before you have an intervention, you perform a risk assessment of
every individual; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: And if a person is assessed as being high risk, they're referred on to an
appropriate authority - law enforcement, some other authority; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: Could I take you to paragraph 21 of your statement. Do you have that
there?
MR BRENNAN: Yes.

MR SHERMAN: You have set out here the difference risk factors and vulnerabilities that
individuals in different age groups exhibit. Is this based on your own personal observations or
that of your staff?
MR BRENNAN: It's from a combination of my existing work within the field, some
research that was done initially when we were sort of conducting and sort of doing our sort of
referral pathways, but as well it's some of the key risk factors that we have observed within
the work that we have done.
MR SHERMAN: Do these different risk and vulnerability factors feed into the way that you
stage interventions with these different groups?
MR BRENNAN: Yes. Because we've found in the past it's sort of vital to make sure that we
are tailoring the program to the needs of the individual, and these are the ones that we noticed
that do impact on to the individuals and probably have the most impact on to their
engagement or likelihood of disengaging.
MR SHERMAN: I think at paragraph 20, you indicate that you receive either self-referrals
or referrals from third parties such as families or professionals. To what extent do they
remain involved once they've referred a person?
MR BRENNAN: So you might see in the later aspects of our work that we do is we are
actually looking at ways that we can increase - especially for family-led interventions or
family referrals, ways that we can continue to support the families and ways that we can
continue to support those individuals. So we actually like to try to continue to incorporate
them into it and use them as that sort of building block, as we said, to have that wraparound
service for an individual.
MR SHERMAN: Certainly. Now, I just wanted to take you through some of ReRoute's
program and have you explain them to us. So we might start with the intervention programs,
which I think commence at paragraph 27 of your statement. Could you just briefly tell us
what the common denominator is among all of those programs, what brings them together?
MR BRENNAN: Yes. So our intervention programs are the ones that we are looking at
providing that direct service to individuals that have been referred. So these are what we refer
to as that direct line intervention and sort of working on that behaviour change aspect. So
when we are looking at it, our mentoring provides a level of support, a level of sort of
continued engagement for our individuals, and our Reintegration Program complements that
by looking at the different so psychosocial factors that may have led an individual to become
involved in one of these movements or ideologies. So those work really hand in hand to
actually look at ways we can help this individual, ways that they can provide to psycho
education, that positive role modelling and as well those direct services that are likely to
shape an individual's experience to moving out of an ideologically or religiously-motivated
group, as well as lastly, for that Employment Program, that is working as that final
complementary point to sort of work to allow individuals to gain access to what is ultimately
a very vital part of their disengagement process and hopefully reintegrate back into
a pro-social and pro-community environment.

MR SHERMAN: And so the idea is they are community-based mentors; is that right?
MR BRENNAN: Yes. So we utilise mentors that are perceived to have characteristics or
experience that would be viewed as being desirable or able to provide that sort of level of
support and mentoring to individuals, but they are from the community.
MR SHERMAN: And why is that done? Is that perceived to be something that enables the
mentor to have greater access or greater impact on the individual? Is that the thinking?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: Okay. And then in terms of the Reintegration Program, that's a case
management style program; is that correct?
MR BRENNAN: That's correct.
MR SHERMAN: And could you explain in general terms what it does?
MR BRENNAN: So our case managers in the Reintegration Program look at existing
programs that might already exist out there in the community - so this might be mental health
services, it might be substance use services or even education providers - and looks at areas
that we could look at engaging the individual to sort of integrate them back into the
community, so gaining them access and gaining them pathways to engaging with and
reducing some of those psychosocial barriers that they may have had initially or that was
identified as part of the initial referral in. As well as they work to provide that sort of
guidance and assistance to our mentors. So it might be looking at specific others or specific
things they could look at that actually assist as part of their Mentoring Program. So it might
be around making recommendations to engage with an education group, a community group
or even experience a sort of exposure to museums or what we refer to as other community
groups that they might have previously had grievances with in the past. So it's identifying
areas that they can ultimately address a lot of those psychosocial barriers.
MR SHERMAN: And so the Mentoring Program and the Reintegration Programs case
management aspect work kind of together; is that fair?
MR BRENNAN: Correct.
MR SHERMAN: Then there's an Employment Program which helps individuals gain stable
and rewarding employment opportunities. Why is that an important feature of the
intervention?
MR BRENNAN: Because what we have found a lot in the past, especially when we are
looking at our ideologically-motivated extremism, there has always been a rhetoric around
the fact that individuals from what is perceived as your Caucasian backgrounds aren't
receiving a level of support or aren't receiving a level of assistance that might be perceived as
one of their targeted grievances groups, whereas we are sort of looking at providing programs

where they are ultimately able to gain access to that. And employment has been seen as a real
core fundamental aspect of it, because when they have stable and access to stable
employment, it opens up the other areas that we can engage within the community. It opens
up their sort of pathways towards reintegration for it.
However, sometimes in the past when we are looking at areas if they have had offending
history in the past, it has been very difficult for them to either engage or maintain
employment in the past. So we're looking at ways that we can support and integrate them into
these ones and also provide that mentoring for them as well, so when we are engaging with
our mentors as part of the employment program, it is actually able to provide them with
a stable basis to where, if they are potentially still engaging with some of these
ideologically-motivated groups, that they can maintain that mentoring aspect around how
they might continue to be employed or maintain employment out there in the community
without this impacting on to them.
MR SHERMAN: So when you referred to the perception earlier about people of Caucasian
extract not being supported, is that really a point about addressing the grievance that they
have as a radicalised individual, that the employment relationship addresses that particular
grievance? Is that -
MR BRENNAN: Correct. In one aspect of it. Because when we have had a situation in the
past where they might hold on to these belief systems that aren't actually based on sort of any
evidence in the past, if we are able to provide them with a real-world example they do have
access and it is actually support that is available to them, it removes one element of,
potentially, that grievance that they've held in the past.
MR SHERMAN: If I could direct your attention to paragraph 42 where you address the next
category of programs, which is proactive programs, these include the Sports program, the
Starting the Conversation program, the Safe to Support program, the Safe to Exit program.
I would just like to discuss some of those programs with you as well. The Sports Program is

the attacks overtly. And this group was definitely one of them. They were - they were very
jubilant.
But as the night - you know, the conversations went on, you know, one of my friends asked
him that, "I understand jihad but flying planes into buildings, like, where is that?" And the
guy said, the mouthpiece, you know, he said, "Well, they're all kuffar anyway so it doesn't
matter. They are fair targets." And then both of us kind of side-eyed each other like, "I don't
buy that", and that was - those were the conversations that I was having that day.
MS HAMMOND: And in your statement, you talk about as you've said now, being disturbed
by some of the things that were being said by your peers and that having an impact on you at
that time as well.
MR SHAIKH: Yes, absolutely.
MS HAMMOND: So you mentioned that as a result of that experience, you decided to seek
more formal Islamic study. Could you explain to the Commission how you went about doing
that?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. Interesting, because this kind of raises the question of how people end
up where they end up. And so I thought about going to Saudi Arabia to study. Thankfully,
I didn't go. But I was - I think I was 25 by this time, and that's too old for the Saudi Salafi
establishment. They like them young, and they want their minds to be malleable. I was 25.
I mean, there's no hope for me in that regard. So Saudi Arabia was out of the question.
I looked into Egypt. Egypt at the time was too expensive. And it just so happened that the
mosque that - my father was actually running the mosque and was a director of the mosque,
and there was construction happening in the mosque, and a couple of the labourers that were
there were from Syria, and they heard I was looking to go and study.

And so one of them said, you know, "I have a home there in Syria. My sister and her family
live there. Why don't you go to Syria and I won't even charge you rent because you are
a student of knowledge. I will get divine rewards from God because I am supporting a student
of knowledge." And so I said I guess I'm going to Syria. And so I - it took me some months, a
few months. I sold all my belongings. I got rid of everything, liquidated as much as I could
and bought a plane ticket. And I went first, set up shop, got my residency permit and then my
wife and my two very young children at the time followed.
MS HAMMOND: I understand you ultimately spent approximately two years in Syria; is
that right?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, I would spend - ended up spending two years studying the subjects.
MS HAMMOND: You've spoken that at that time you were particularly exposed to the
Orthodox Sufi tradition. Can you briefly explain what that tradition is?
MR SHAIKH: I love to use the analogy. I see the Sufis as the Jedi of the Muslim world, and
I see the Salafis and the Wahhabis as the Sith. And so I see them as benevolent. I see the
others as malevolent. Their perspective was completely different. And, mind you, I showed
up to Syria at that time, a real police state - you know, the war criminal Bashar al-Assad was
still in power at that time. And unbeknownst to me, I was this, you know, the spoiled
Canadian, you know, who went thinking, "You know, these kuffar western countries, they are
so evil and bad" and I end up in a real police state - even though it's a Muslim country but,
you know, just some of the horror stories that I heard there. But at least the Sufis had a very
positive disposition. And I showed up with this, you know, turban, beard, long robes and very
quickly realised, like, people don't dress like that over there. I was actually the - I stood out
like a sore thumb.
So a lot of them, they could see that this guy is a Salafist. In fact, the question that they asked
me in my entrance interview was, "Are you a Sufi or are you a Salafi?" And I knew that they
wanted the right answer and so I said, "No, no, I'm a Sufi, I'm not a Salafi." But I had just,
you know, just left that Salafi understanding, I guess. So that's how I understood the
Orthodox Sufis to be. They are observant Muslims and they're just really, really nice people.
MS HAMMOND: So you describe in your statement how your religious and spiritual ideas
fundamentally changed as a result of your time in Syria. And you say that rather than
defining yourself through conflict and militancy, you came to see your faith as centred on
compassion and positive engagement with others. Is that a fair summary of your time in Syria
and the impact it had on you?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. I used to wear glasses at the time. I got laser eye surgery since then. But
the Sheikh, you know, he said to me, "I'm going to give you a new pair of glasses by which to
view the world". And he just - he kept it simple for me. In the Islamic tradition, there is one
of - there's a body of literature called the Hadith Qudsi, which is, you know, the statements of
God but on the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Like the Qur'an is considered the
speech of God. The Hadith is the speech of the Prophet, peace be upon him, but the Hadith

Qudsi is still the - not the speech of God. It's the words of God but the speech of the Prophet.
And the first Hadith Qudsi is when God creates, he creates the pen. He tells the pen, "Write".
The pen says "What should I write?" And God says, "Write that my mercy prevails over my
wrath."
And then he said, so, look, the first - this is the first Hadith Qudsi. Then he says, "Before you
start reading the Qur'an, you invoke the name of God, full of grace, full of mercy." So there
you go. And then third, the Prophet - peace be upon him - is referred to as a mercy to the
world. So he just said to me that if you are not starting with mercy and grace then you are not
doing it right. And so that really impacted me, because he went straight to the text and the
scripture, and I couldn't argue with that.
MS HAMMOND: Mr Shaikh, after your time in Syria, you returned to Canada and there
was a very interesting portion in your life that I propose not to ask you in any particular detail
about, but is it correct that you, in fact, then spent a considerable period working with the
Canadian Security Intelligence Service and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as an
undercover operative infiltrating jihadist cells and then subsequently was involved as a
witness in the prosecution of a number of jihadists arrested in Canada?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, that's correct. Just very quickly, I had returned back to Canada, and the
first week that I got back, in the newspaper, the first Canadian was arrested on terrorism
charges. Momin Khawaja was arrested in connection with the 2004 London fertiliser bomb
plot, a year before the Underground attacks. Momin Khawaja sat to the left of me in the
Qur'an school I went to as a kid. I grew up with him. We played Hot Wheels cars together.
And so I thought it was a mistake that they arrested him. I didn't realise also the difference in
the jurisdictions of the Security Intelligence and Federal Police. But, yes, I saw - I mean
maybe some of you remember, once upon a time, these things called phone books where
people's names, addresses and phone numbers were available on every street corner, well in
the back of it, there is government listings, and I saw the Canadian Security Intelligence
Service and picked up the phone and I called.
MS HAMMOND: And you reached out to them. So then after that period in your life, I think
you also then spent a considerable period working with the United States government on
various activities to counter ISIS and spent some time doing that?
MR SHAIKH: Yes.
MS HAMMOND: But then I understand since 2016, you have been involved with an
organisation called Parents4Peace. I'm wondering if you could explain to the Commission
what Parents4Peace does?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. And just keep in mind that this was the height of the ISIS period.
Really, ISIS, we started to see the rise of ISIS in 2012. By 2014, they had declared their
so-called caliphate. And there was this discussion about what to do with young people who
had gone to join them, and, of course, the understanding that they were at some point going to
return back. And there were a couple of clusters of people who had gone to join them. Some

who went pre-2014, some who came back shortly thereafter. Some who came back after 2014
and others who had travelled after 2014 and remained.
So it was at the height of this that the whole CVE concept was born. You know, it was
President Obama at the time. There was a CVE summit at the White House. And this is when
CVE was born. And so a lot of the programs that came out at that time, were, you know,
some of the programs that we have been talking about - you've all been talking about, this is
when they started to be formed and were kind of starting to get their footing. So in by 2016,
this organisation Parents4Peace had just recently been formed.
It was initially founded by an African-American man, may he rest in peace. He died not too
long ago. But the Melvin Bledsoe, his son has radicalised. His son travelled to Yemen,
returned back from Yemen. The father was very, you know, very much into African
American history. He told me how, you know, Marcus Garvey, for example, you know, his
photo was in the house. And now his son was like, no, no, no, we don't keep pictures in the
home. And so the father was observing some of these warning signs. But worst of all, what
his son ended up doing was he committed a drive-by shooting at a military recruiting centre,
killing two service members. And so he was, of course, apprehended, arrested, and is now
serving a life sentence.
But Melvin, you know, kind of looked out and looked to see where he could get support, and
he must - he said, "I'm sure other parents are going through this and where do they go", and
he found that there was nothing that parents could reach out to. There was no one that could
help him. And so he started this organisation. Myrieme Churchill, she is the executive
director. She reached out to me. She saw what I had been doing online with a lot of these
ISIS individuals. I was debating them online openly. I was trolling some of them, tracking
a whole bunch of them, and so she thought that - you know, I think you should start working
with the organisation and start formalising what I was doing.
MS HAMMOND: You've described your role with Parents4Peace as an interventionist and
as a Former. Can you explain what those roles involve?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. So I'll start with Former. So we use Former with a capital F for
individuals who were part of violent extremist movements and have since, you know, left
those movements. And not just left, but have also practised the, you know, the activity of
producing other Formers, so encouraging people also to leave these violent extremist
movements. The interventionism - because you don't need to be a Former to be an
interventionist. And so the Former is one category that I fall into, and the interventionist is
really the work that we have been doing. And I use my experiences as a Former in my
intervention work.
MS HAMMOND: And can you briefly summarise what your intervention work looks like?
I understand you work on a one-on-one basis with individuals usually?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. So we - it's an NGO. It's a non-government organisation. And it's
overwhelmingly funded by private philanthropy, grants and others. We did recently get
funding from the United States Department of Homeland Security in their Targeted Violence

and Terrorism Prevention Program. And we have a helpline as well, and, you know, people
will call the helpline. So it could be from what I categorise as the pre-criminal space and
post-criminal space. Pre-criminal space before charges have been laid. So a teacher might see
something. Parents, overwhelmingly, or intimate bystanders is the term, they may see
something. It could be an aunt. It could be a parent. You know, in the case of QAnon, which
was a conspiracy theory that people were having, we had, like, middle-aged children who
were calling about their elderly parents who were being sucked into some of these conspiracy
theories. So it was a pathway that people could reach out to us.
In the post-criminal space, it's usually lawyers who reach out to us because their clients have
been arrested in a criminal matter, or sometimes the FBI will reach out to us because the FBI
generally don't like to prosecute, investigate juveniles, and so they may, you know, either
show up at the parents' home and give us - give them our business card or refer a case to us
and say, hey, you know, why don't you guys reach out to the parents independently and bring
to bear your services. So that's the catchment method. And then it goes through the intake
process. There's a number of questions that are asked. There's an embedded threat and risk
assessment in that.
It is then brought to the case consult. It is then assigned to usually two interventionists. So
while I am a Former, there is another Former who is a Former neo-Nazi and, but we also have
social workers, trained social workers, trained psychologists, who also we kind of team up on
cases and then, yes, we do this one-on-one approach. Now, there are different approaches one
can take in this. Like, I've also done a certified peer supporter certification. And even how the
peer support becomes relevant is in the mental health field, it's usually substance abuse and
mental health and somebody who has gone through one or both of those things and is able to
help others who are going through, that from the perspective of, "Hey, I have been where
you're at. Let me try to help you." So there are different techniques that we use. That peer
support model is, or approach, or a technique, and motivational interviewing,
psycho-education, and so that's how we do the one-on-ones with.
MS HAMMOND: Based on your experience, are you able to speak to the Commission about
what it is that you consider makes interventions effective with a person?
MR SHAIKH: I think the most effective component is to be genuine. I learned this because,
in some cases when I'm talking - I have spoken to a juvenile or whatever, and when they
realise that I used to be an undercover, that becomes an aggravating factor for them. They are
like, well, why would I talk to you; you are like the enemy. I was talking to one guy who was
arrested in a sting operation with an undercover, and when we started talking, he - at the end
of it, he told his lawyer that, "I'm not going to talk to Mubin until he repents to Allah for what
he has done."
So I came back - I lost a lot of sleep over that, let me tell you. But I came back and I basically
explained to him that I used to be that, and I know how they work and how they operate, and
I'm here because I wish that I had somebody to talk to when I was your age. So just making it
very realistic and true for that person, I think, worked a lot because then when we were done
with everything, he considered me a part of his family.

So being genuine, I think, is the most important factor in it. Being knowledgeable and also
being observant, especially in my context of Islamist-related cases, because I always tell
them, you know, I said you're not going to out-Muslim me. You know, I pray more than you
do. You just can't, you can't catch up to me in that regard. So it shows that I walk the walk.
And because for a lot of these guys who, for whatever reason they're looking for that rigidity,
and a lot of times, you know, they - it's - they're trying and they kind of present like I'm really
religious but really they're not.
So I think the genuineness or authenticity, the observance and then using those techniques in
a sophisticated manner. So it's basically all these tools that we have in a toolbox that we
know which tool to apply in that particular context, depending on that individual. If I have,
for example, a juvenile, he was 14 years old when he first got arrested, autism spectrum
disorder, right. And it was a learning curve for me to understand how ASD appears in a case
with a juvenile. It's a spectrum, so it can appear in very different ways. And me, who was
used to debating people and very cognitive, very theological, now you're faced with a young
juvenile who it is not cognitive at all; it's very mechanical. It's very black and white thinking.
It's, you know, so I had to shift the way in which I approached him.
And so I think this is really the most important approach and methodology, and that is to (1)
have all those tools, and there is a number of tools that you need to have, understanding of
ideologies, understanding of - you know, I went and did a Concurrent Disorders Certificate
from the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto because I wanted to understand,
like, how do these things interplay with each other. Sometimes you have a person with
mental disease and they are using substances, narcotics.
MS HAMMOND: So it's about meeting the person where their needs -
MR SHAIKH: Yes.
MS HAMMOND: - are and being responsive. Commissioner, I'm mindful of the time. I
think we can probably conclude this evidence within about 10 minutes, if you're content to
take lunch a little bit later.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, we will press on.
MS HAMMOND: Mr Shaikh, I wonder if you could speak briefly about the role of
community and social supports in effective disengagement and deradicalisation?
MR SHAIKH: Community and social supports. Yes, depends on where the community - like
what community we are referring to; right? So in - and, again, Parents4Peace, we deal with
all ideologies across the board. We don't, we're not, we don't fixate on any one. We're equal
opportunity in that regard. And so depending on where the individual is coming from, that
will determine what kinds of community supports they need.
So in this case of the juvenile 14 year old ASD, he was - he was marginalised. He was
isolated from his community - from his, sorry, his peer group at school. You know, he has an
affect that is observable. So other people would see him and they're like, yeah, something's

not right with this kid. So he was marginalised from his peer group. And now he took on this,
you know, extremist rigid ideology and so, at the end of the day, he just needed friends that
accepted him for who he was. And so, in his case - and it's rare, but I actually flew out to see
him in person and physically took him to the mosque and introduced him to the people there.
And so - and now he is doing great because he has people that support him. You know, they
understand that he - you know, he has these needs.
And so we will kind of do warm referrals as well. We're not - you know, we have the ability
and I guess we are able to be more proactive that we can actually do warm referrals to things.
So it just depends on what they need. Sometimes they, you know, they might just need to go,
you know, to a gym or they might - they might need further support, psychiatrists and other
professionals.
MS HAMMOND: Yes. I have two further questions. The first is whether you can explain,
based on your experience, what you see as the role of antisemitism in relation to extremist
ideologies?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, we, Parents4Peace actually just recently, we did kind of carve out
a specific intervention for antisemitic-related cases. So when we do that intake and the case
consult, and we see that the greater ideological influence here is some kind of antisemitic
belief, we will put it in what we call the Antisemitism Intervention Recovery Program. And
what we've seen also is that 70 per cent of our cases show some kind of antisemitic influence.
Of course, you know, you do have some people who are - you know, if it's like a straight
neo-Nazi, you know, it's not - of course, they hate Muslims too and coloured people, black
people, brown people, but the antisemitism is front and centre when it comes to that. In other
cases, the antisemitism is just one of a number of hateful ideas that they may have. But it
does - antisemitism appears to be the connective tissue across extremist ideologies.
MS HAMMOND: You bring this very particular perspective of having now worked for
many years in this space but also having your own experience of radicalisation as a young
man. From where you sit now, are you able to reflect on what might have been effective for
you as a young man and what might have diverted you from the path that you did ultimately
follow in the 1990s?
MR SHAIKH: Yes. This is a common question that's asked, and I was thinking about this.
And we would like to think that if only this kid could have had a mentor or somebody that
could explain these things for them. And I'm sure that - that is true in many cases. But we
should also be - we should also understand that sometimes there's nothing you can do.
A young person needs to engage with these ideas, and they will just come to believe those
ideas, and there isn't anything you can say to them. Because I can recall when I was in my
extremist mentality and there were people who came to me trying, no, look, brother this is not
really Islam, this is extreme, blah, blah, blah, I didn't want to hear it. Because I was like, this
is what I need to do and this is what I'm going to do.
And so there is a period of that rigidity that's there. However, why I think it is important that
we try whatever we can is because some of those things that those people said while I thought
that I was ignoring them and just brushing them aside, later on, their ideas and their

arguments started to - started to echo in my mind again and I started to think about those
things. So we have to be - we have to understand that it can be effective and many times it is,
but understanding also that sometimes it may just fall on deaf ears.
MS HAMMOND: And that may be because, in your understanding, it's not until there is one
of those cognitive opening moments that someone might be more -
MR SHAIKH: That's absolutely right, -
MS HAMMOND: - receptive?
MR SHAIKH: - yes.
MS HAMMOND: Commissioner, I have no further questions for Mr Shaikh. I understand
Mr Bender may.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. But perhaps just before you, Mr Bender. Mr Shaikh you grew up
in a household where the family didn't agree with having kuffars at home; is that right?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, the uncle was particularly -
COMMISSIONER: And what about your parents?
MR SHAIKH: My parents were okay but I don't think they would have been okay with the
house party.
COMMISSIONER: Right. And did you know, when you were at school, Jewish students
that you were aware of?
MR SHAIKH: No. There was - there was one Jewish student, or one Jewish person in the
Army Cadets that I was in. But nothing -
COMMISSIONER: Did you have a particular attitude towards him?
MR SHAIKH: No. No, did not have any issues with him. It's really only when I decided to
take on the ideology that I was being told, listen, you got be - you got to hate the Jews, you
got to hate everybody. So it was something that I kind of forced on to myself.
COMMISSIONER: Mr Bender.
MR BENDER SC: Thank you, Commissioner. Mr Shaikh, there was some evidence heard
yesterday about a distinction when disengaging a person from violent extremism between, on
the one hand, taking steps that might stop mobilising them towards violence and, on the other
hand, changing their private beliefs. You are somebody who himself has been deradicalised
and continues to work in deradicalisation. How important do you consider it is to have the
private beliefs of the person at risk changed during the program?

MR SHAIKH: Very, very important and, I mean, I think foundational. And I understand
government agencies can't do that, but this is why I think the NGO model works particularly
well, because we can do that and we do do that. At least we try. Sometimes it depends.
I can't - like this juvenile kid, he is inclined towards the Salafist view, but it's a more
moderate Salafist view, so I'm happy to leave him in that. But where we can change the
views, we try.
MR BENDER SC: While attempting to prevent somebody from becoming a violent
extremist or persuading them to stop being a violent extremist, why is it so important to
change their private beliefs?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, if you think to the basic - basic concept of psychology, you know,
thoughts precede actions and beliefs are part of thoughts. And if you believe that it is
legitimate to do X, then for them to not do X, you need to change the belief that underpins the
intention towards that action.
MR BENDER SC: Thank you. In your evidence, you have referred a number of times to
your own deradicalisation and to deradicalisation programs. Can we take it from that, that
you don't see any particular problem with referring to deradicalisation programs as such, that
is, as "deradicalisation"?
MR SHAIKH: Yes, that's the term that was invented, I guess, and that's the term that we use.
But if people want to use other terms, I mean, they're free to, but as long as we understand
what that underlying activity of "deradicalisation" is. It is a cognitive shift. Disengagement is
a behavioural shift where the ideas still remain, but deradicalisation is the word that
everybody uses.
MR BENDER SC: Thank you, Mr Shaikh. Thank you, Commissioner.

MS HAMMOND: No, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you very much, Mr Shaikh.
MR SHAIKH: Thank you, Madam Commissioner.
